title: Analytic spread complexity in three-level systems and the spacing-ratio distribution
abstract: The spread complexity characterizes the spreading of a quantum state over the Krylov basis and has been proposed to capture the correlations between energy levels. How such correlations manifest in the dynamics has been studied mainly numerically for large matrices. Here we consider three-level systems, the smallest setting with spacing correlations, and derive exact results for the spread complexity, the Krylov variance, and the Krylov entropy. At infinite temperature, the Krylov basis depends on the spectrum only through the ratio of consecutive level spacings, and the spectral variance enters only as an overall time scale. For Gaussian ensembles, these variables are statistically independent, and the averaged spread complexity and variance reduce to one-dimensional integrals over the spacing-ratio distribution encoding the level statistics. We establish universal late-time values of the complexity and variance, and an algebraic relaxation with exponents set by the Dyson index. We also outline the extension to $d$ levels, with the ensemble-averaged spread complexity expressed as a $(d-2)$-dimensional integral over the joint distribution of consecutive spacing ratios.

title: Quantum violation of Causal Friendliness in the instrumental scenario
abstract: How far can quantum theory depart from a classical worldview? Bell inequality violations show that no theory can simultaneously uphold absoluteness of observed events, freedom of choice, relativistic causality, and classical causal explanations. While generalized notions of causality, capable of incorporating quantum resources, can account for Bell correlations, the Local Friendliness theorem showed that, in extended Wigner's friend scenarios, the conflict between quantum theory and causal explanations persists even after classical causality is abandoned. This revealed a new form of nonclassicality stronger than what was revealed by Bell's theorem. However, Local Friendliness has been confined to Bell causal structures so far, and it remains unknown whether a related form of nonclassicality persists in more general causal networks. Here we answer this question by considering a Wigner's friend version of the instrumental network, a paradigmatic causal structure in which communication between parties is allowed, and, unlike the Bell scenario, relativistic causality does not impose any restriction. We show, both theoretically and in a proof-of-principle photonic experiment, that quantum correlations are incompatible with Causal Friendliness, which is the conjunction of the absoluteness of observed events and the generalized nonclassical causal constraints imposed by the network. Such constraints extend relativistic causality from Bell scenarios to networks of arbitrary structure. These results establish a form of quantum nonclassicality stronger than previously observed in instrumental-network violations of classical causality, generalizing Local Friendliness beyond Bell-Wigner scenarios and uncovering a new class of correlations with potential applications in future quantum technologies.

title: Fast mixing and thermal phases from strong decay of correlations
abstract: We show that a strong form of correlation decay in quantum Gibbs states has far-reaching dynamical consequences. For a smooth path of geometrically local commuting Hamiltonians whose Gibbs states satisfy strong decay of correlations, we construct $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Lindbladian evolutions exactly connecting these states in both directions, together with $\mathrm{O}(1)$-time quasi-local Hamiltonian evolutions exactly connecting their canonical purifications. These quasi-local connections strengthen previously known quantum-channel circuit constructions based on the decay of connected correlation functions [R. Ma, V. Khemani, and S. Sang, PRX Quantum 7, 033052 (2026)], which approximately connect states within the same phase but have depths that grow logarithmically with system size. Furthermore, if the Gibbs-state path contains a product state, we prove that the single-site Glauber dynamics has a $Ω(1)$ spectral gap independent of the system size throughout the path. This establishes Glauber-dynamics fast mixing for models that may violate the strong spatial mixing condition used in prior proofs, including (1) the $q$-state Potts model throughout the high-temperature phase for any $q$ and any finite dimension; (2) the Ising model with a longitudinal field at low temperature, with frustrating perturbations that destroy monotonicity of the dynamics; and (3) the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory at low temperatures comparing to a field perturbation, even though the model supports classical memories at intermediate temperatures. Intriguingly, we establish fast mixing of these classical Markov chains using tools from quantum physics like Lieb-Robinson bounds.

title: Optically-induced electric Aharonov-Bohm effect
abstract: Although it was proposed almost 70 years ago, the electric version of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect, where the interference pattern of quantum charged particles is affected by electric fields that do not interact locally with them, was never experimentally implemented. Here we propose a feasible way to experimentally verify such an important effect, for an electron double-slit interferometer with the slits carved in a nonlinear crystal. The AB phase is generated by a quasi-DC electric field induced in the crystal with the passage of a light pulse (the optical rectification effect) while the electron is superposed in the two slits. We show that this procedure can change the interference pattern of a ensemble of electrons even if they are subjected to negligible electric fields during their propagation, considering feasible parameters.

title: QuantumInputOutput.jl: A Julia framework for input-output theory with quantum pulses and the SLH formalism
abstract: The interaction of traveling photonic pulses with quantum systems is a fundamental process for many quantum technologies such as quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols. The so-called SLH formalism, named for the triple of operators that parametrize the dynamics, in combination with virtual emission and absorption cavities provides a general toolbox to describe such processes. However, modeling open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses becomes cumbersome once several components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. Here we present QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source framework that automates this derivation process: first, symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are derived using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. Next, the obtained operators are converted to (time-dependent) numerical matrices or are used to obtain higher-order mean-field equations. The numerical expressions are presented in a form immediately suitable for solving the time evolution of the master equation and analyzing the output modes via correlation functions. Besides its usefulness for numerical simulations, the framework also provides a convenient tool to derive symbolic expressions for one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.

title: Efficient quantum-circuit simulation of classical control of computational order
abstract: We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on $N$ independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most $N^2$ queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional $N^2-N$ queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.

title: The radical pair mechanism can generate nuclear-spin entanglement
abstract: The radical pair mechanism is a quantum-mechanical process underlying weak magnetic field effects in chemical and biological systems. While nuclear polarization and electronic entanglement in this mechanism have been studied extensively, the possibility of creating entanglement between nuclear spins has, to the best of our knowledge, remained unexplored. Here, we show that nuclear-spin entanglement can develop from initially maximally mixed nuclear spin states and evolve over repeated radical pair cycles. Its generation and persistence depend on the initial electronic state, the available reaction channels, and the interplay between recombination rates, hyperfine interactions, and the magnetic field. We demonstrate this behaviour in both a minimal two-nucleus model and a five-nucleus model inspired by the photosynthetic radical pair P700--$A_1$. Radical pair mechanism generated nuclear-spin entanglement offers a potential new resource for quantum technologies and opens avenues for exploring its role in biological systems.

title: Probing Spatiotemporal Quantum Correlations with Two-Qubit Relaxometry
abstract: Quantum impurities and spin qubits are powerful local probes of magnetic fluctuations, but conventional relaxometry reduces their information to a local relaxation rate at a single frequency. Building on advances in two-qubit sensing of spatial correlations, we show how two complementary protocols probe finite-time correlations in interacting quantum matter. Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates the signed contribution of correlated relaxation to the joint ground-state population. To second order in the probe-environment coupling, the resulting population contrast measures a finite-time integral of the energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance probes the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable frequency window. For a gapless quantum spin chain, the signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation. Luttinger-liquid theory links sign changes as the qubit frequency is swept to the propagation time between the probes. It also predicts distinct spatial power laws for the Bell signal before the correlation front and at late times, when the sensing window resolves the qubit frequency. Matrix-product-state calculations for the spin chain test the pre-front scaling at zero and finite magnetization and extract the propagation velocity from Bell oscillations at zero magnetization. The probe coupling geometry determines which spin and momentum sectors contribute to the measured signals.

title: Finite-time spectral enhancement of transient quantum thermometry
abstract: Transient quantum thermometry extracts temperature information before a probe reaches thermal equilibrium. We study how finite interaction times affect thermometric precision for a harmonic-oscillator probe prepared in a number state and weakly coupled to a thermal bosonic reservoir. A second-order time-convolutionless master equation retains the finite-time reservoir response, allowing modes away from the probe frequency to shape the populations and their temperature dependence. For the baseline parameters, this response raises the quantum Fisher information about fivefold above the Markovian prediction, in agreement with an exact solution of the model. When the probability of leaving the initial state is small, we derive an analytical condition for this enhancement. To assess its operational significance, we examine the temperature information acquired per unit time. Under the exact dynamics, this rate is largest within the reservoir memory time. With negligible preparation and readout overhead, the optimum is about five times the best Markovian rate and 30 times an upper bound on the equilibrium rate. The advantage survives smooth switching, although overhead and longer coupling ramps reduce it.

title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz
abstract: The recursive quantum approximate optimisation algorithm~(RQAOA) shrinks an unconstrained combinatorial optimisation problem by eliminating one variable at a time, guided by correlations measured in variational quantum states. We extend this recursion to constrained problems by building on the quantum alternating operator ansatz, which restricts the evolution to feasible solutions through a feasible initial state and feasibility-preserving mixers. However, every elimination alters the feasibility structure, so that such a mixer for the original problem generally fails to be one for the subproblems. Previous extensions to Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover sidestep this with tailored reduction rules that keep every subproblem within the original problem class. We resolve this by identifying, for a given constraint structure, a broader problem class that is closed under all eliminations, and by efficiently constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for every class member. We do so for monotone constraints, such as for the knapsack problem, for linear equality constraints with polynomially bounded weights, including Hamming weight constraints, and for combinations of equality constraints with a single inequality constraint, such as the cardinality-constrained knapsack problem. Conversely, we show that these restrictions cannot be lifted in general without leaving the realm of efficient constructions. Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances demonstrate that our recursive scheme can outperform both its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.

title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control of Superconducting Qubits
abstract: Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented. For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative $Y_{π/2}$ gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below $10^{-4}$, including leakage from the computational subspace. The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed. The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.

title: Magic of Dicke states: density, cost and yield
abstract: Dicke states are an elementary family of many-body quantum states, consisting of equal superpositions of all configurations of $L$ qubits with $n$ excitations. We show that their magic, as measured by the stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE), is extensive at every filling $f=n/L$ except half-filling, and we obtain the magic density analytically, together with the subleading terms. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation, we also investigate the yield of Dicke states, and find that they can produce on average an extensive number of CCZ states (or $T$ states with a catalyst) at any $0<f<1$. This yield is not self-averaging, but fluctuates from run to run by $O(L)$, as if it were set by a hidden phase shared by all qubits. At half-filling, the SRE grows only logarithmically, while the preparation cost, average yield and relative entropy of magic remain extensive, so that a small SRE does not necessarily signal a weak resource. These results can be understood by viewing the Dicke state as a fixed-magnetization projection of a product of tilted spins.

title: Linear monitoring-feedback Model for Linearized gravity
abstract: Whether gravity has quantum degrees of freedom is a question of fundamental importance. We formulate a linear monitoring-feedback framework for gravitational interactions that includes local classical-record models of semiclassical gravity and, when quantum resources are supplied in correlated ancilla inputs, can reproduce linearized quantum-gravity dynamics. Auxiliary systems monitor the positions of massive bodies, and their records are fed back through a chosen gravitational response kernel. At the level of linear input-output theory, this construction makes the deterministic response explicit while exposing the force noise and correlations associated with the auxiliary sector. We organize the allowed ancilla correlations into three regimes. In Regime-I, independent ancillas have unsqueezed, uncorrelated sensing and back-action quadratures. A single object then has a minimum classical-gravity noise (CGN), S_F^min = 2 hbar M Omega_SN^2, where Omega_SN is the Schrodinger-Newton frequency set by the microscopic mass distribution. In Regime-II, arbitrary local sensing--back-action correlations are allowed, but the ancillas associated with different objects remain independent. The single-object CGN is then unrestricted, while the joint force-noise matrix obeys a determinant bound that is equivalent to the local classical-channel/no-entanglement bound. In Regime-III, cross-object correlations and a common nonlocal mediator are allowed. The commuting force noises can then be jointly squeezed, entanglement between the masses can occur, and--with a suitable retarded response and input state--the monitoring-feedback system can reproduce the noise and commutators of linearized quantum gravity, including non-Markovian quantum fluctuations.

title: Quantum Data Processing Unit for Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
abstract: Quantum computers need real-time classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback within device-specific timing constraints. We introduce the quantum data processing unit (QDPU), an architecture between a quantum device and its controller. Its core is a machine-learned quantum data model (QDM), adapted to the measurement response and noise characteristics of the device. We implement an FPGA pipeline for neutral-atom array assembly that performs occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling in FPGA logic. One calibrated matched-filter lane classifies a $50\times50$ array in 12.5 $μ$s. An atom-loss model using a software reference planner evaluates a $35\times35$ target with a 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom. Removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises the predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces the wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s. A GPU-based outer loop is proposed for refitting model parameters between runs. Its NVQLink transport is measured on the board: over 10 GbE to an NVIDIA DGX Spark, the median FPGA-to-host-to-FPGA round trip is 2.74 $μ$s for 128-byte messages forwarded by a CPU core. A separate 12-bit learned qLDPC kernel is placed and routed for the same FPGA target, with a derived latency of 0.84 ms per round for a $[[1122,148]]$ lifted-product code under code-capacity noise. A quantised GraphMP ranking kernel for the same code runs on the board with a median host-to-FPGA-to-host latency of 50.5 $μ$s with one shot in flight, excluding host-side BP+OSD post-processing. Together, these implementations illustrate a shared architecture with workload-specific models and timing requirements.

title: Fast forward-and-backward creation of non-equilibrium Gibbs state in driven dissipative quantum systems
abstract: We present the fast-forward (FF) approach to adiabatic time evolution of an open dissipative quantum system within the framework of the Gorini-Kosaakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. Taking a harmonic oscillator (HO) and a quantum spin as prototype systems under a rapid change of the driving field and in contact with the heat reservoir, we reveal the protocol which creates the non-equilibrium Gibbs state. After preparing the Gibbs state under the fixed external field in advance, we begin to change adiabatically the field. To keep a quasi-adiabatic version of the Gibbs state as the solution of GKSL equation, we solve the inverse problem to obtain the non-adiabatic corrections both to Hamiltonian and to the dissipator. Then we apply the fast forward-and-backward (abbreviated as FF for convenience) time-rescaling, obtaining the FF variants of both Hamiltonian and detailed balance condition (DBC) among dissipative coefficients. The present scheme generates the time-periodic Gibbs state as if a limit-cycle solution of the innovated GKSL equation under the time-periodic driving field. Thanks to the FF variant of DBC, we see the energy conservation of power and heat current of the system, and reversibility of whole system including a reservoir. The requirement of positivity of the FF dissipative coefficients imposes a constraint on the speed of the FF driving. At low temperature, the upper speed limit of the FF periodic driving is found to be proportional to $\tildeβ^{-1/2}\exp(a\tildeβ)$ with $\tildeβ$ the scaled inverse temperature and $a$ the positive constant of $O(1)$.

title: Multitime Equilibration and Multitime Mpemba Effects
abstract: Equilibration of a quantum state leaves open whether its response to later interventions has also equilibrated. We establish multitime equilibration for a continuous process on a fixed observation window, retaining the autonomous system--environment dynamics and all internal time differences. A finite-time mean-square bound controls the full continuous-process norm through the effective energy dimension and energy-gap correlations. A factorial temporal-order bound lifts fixed-sector convergence to the full process, while a process-visible spectral measure distinguishes mean-square from pointwise equilibration. This framework defines multitime Mpemba effects by comparing preparations relative to one stationary process. In a semicircle-spectrum model, a preparation filter changes the decay exponent from $3/2$ to $5/2$ in every fixed sector and in the summed norm, despite a larger initial distance. A fixed unitary control and terminal measurement exhibit the same exponent improvement in their output probabilities. Noncommuting baths and a many-body spin environment separate this all-sector mechanism from selective finite-time acceleration.

title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Collision Finding over Arbitrary Bounded Types
abstract: We determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding one $r$-collision in an $N$-input function of prescribed type, which specifies all equality-class sizes. For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, we give a tight bound as the maximum of scales determined by the numbers of classes of size at least $2,\ldots,r$. The lower bound holds for a uniformly random function of that type, and a matching algorithm succeeds on every such function. No intermediate class size is required to occur, and every feasible output alphabet is allowed.   The characterization connects the abundant-collision regime associated with set equality to the sparse-target regime of $k$-distinctness. In particular, finding the unique $(k+1)$-collision in type $(k^n,k+1)$ has complexity $Θ_k(N^{3/4-1/[4(2^{k+1}-1)]})$, where $N=kn+k+1$, resolving an open problem of Belovs.   For the lower bound, we introduce a filtered compressed permutation oracle that projects onto a harmonic database subspace after each complete function query. Its $O(T/N)$ comparison error over $T$ queries overcomes the square-root limitation of the unfiltered process. Hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates retain the populations at each intermediate collision order. Matching upper bounds use sampled collision lists and colored adaptive learning graphs, with a coherent decision-to-search conversion that avoids logarithmic overhead. We also give an alternative nested quantum-walk algorithm for three-collision search, matching the bound up to polylogarithmic factors.

title: No universal LOCC entanglement purification
abstract: Entanglement purification aims to obtain high-fidelity entangled states from noisy entangled states. This task becomes particularly challenging when the available input states are finite in number, only partially characterized, and may not be identical. Whether there exists a universal purification protocol applicable to such inputs has therefore been a longstanding question. This motivates the study of universal $n$-to-$1$ entanglement purification. Although no such LOCC protocol exists for the full set of two-qubit entangled states, it has remained open whether this no-go result extends to higher-dimensional bipartite states and multipartite states. In this work, we resolve this question by proving that, for any fixed finite local dimensions, no $n$-to-$1$ LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states. We further show that the bipartite and multipartite no-go results persist under several natural extensions and establish an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations.

title: Local gluing classification and bulk-locked clock rings for $\mathbb{Z}_N$ models on a Klein bottle
abstract: We classify local reflection gluings of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ plaquette model on lattice Klein bottles and solve the obstructed literal seam. Within the monomial far-corner ansatz, all commuting gluings form a family labelled by a unit $u$ of $\mathbb{Z}_N$. They exist for every $N$ at even seam length and, at odd length, exactly when $-1$ is a square modulo $N$. We determine the anyon transport, including exchange seams with $P^2=C$ for charge conjugation $C$, and the relation phases that distinguish an unfrustrated code from a commuting but frustrated Hamiltonian. For the literal gluing, the $2L_x$ noncommuting plaquettes form self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk. This gives an exact reduction of the spectrum to clock-ring spectra, closed-form ring ground energies for $N=2,4$, and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy. We further determine twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains and compare it with logical modules on registered lattice grids; composite dimensions need not give squares of cyclic groups. Dressed-isometry gates and monodromy are reported with their finite-grid scope. Finally, the qudit Gottesman--Knill theorem bounds the computational interpretation: Clifford deformations and Weyl measurements with stabilizer inputs and no external magic states cannot supply a non-stabilizer resource. Charge-conjugation measurements that do supply such states lie outside this operation model. The new results concern explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency and bulk-locked spectra, not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture.

title: Reference-Assisted Qutrit Control and Conditional One-Round Distillation in a Charge-4e Superconductor Model
abstract: We formulate a charge-$4e$ parafermionic-vortex route to qutrit processing as a conditional theory with explicit operational assumptions. Sector preservation and same-label charge-conjugation covariance imply closure for every adaptive visible record. For charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, record probabilities are independent of the supported reference state; for arbitrary inputs, discarding the reference gives a population-weighted mixture of conjugate sector maps. We give a finite-depth stability bound for complete labelled instruments, including postselection and initial zero-sector contamination. A self-contained calculation reproduces the known dense single-qutrit closure of the registered Clifford-plus-Flip gate set. We also specify an abstract ternary CSS $[[11,1,5]]_3$ syndrome/recovery decoder: 243 classical representatives per CSS component correct all 3,609 Pauli errors of support weight at most two, and an exact integer dynamic program yields the full independent-Pauli logical enumerator. Its all-syndrome acceptance is distinct from the known $1/1728$ ideal acceptance of one-round strange-state Golay distillation. An accepted-run target-infidelity budget and a synthetic parameter protocol expose the remaining noise assumptions. Native charge-$4e$ syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, and unconditional fault tolerance are not established.

title: Four-Sector Propagation-Trapping Decomposition and Inverse Design of Initial States in Grover-Coined Quantum Walks on Multiedge Path Graphs
abstract: Controlling propagation and trapping through initial-state preparation requires an explicit relation between the initial amplitudes and the corresponding directional probabilities. We establish this relation for a discrete-time Grover-coined quantum walk on a multiedge path graph with even degree d = 2M, where M is at least 2, and two equal directional blocks. Each block of an arbitrary local state is expressed as its mean component plus a zero-sum deviation. The Grover coin performs a pure exchange of the two block means and reverses the sign of each zero-sum deviation. Together with the graph routing, this gives a unique orthogonal decomposition into four sectors: propagation in opposite directions and bounded trapping on either side of the launch vertex. We derive the four sector probabilities and solve the inverse problem, constructing initial states for any prescribed nonnegative probability quadruple that sums to unity. Explicit representatives are given for d = 4 and d = 6. Sector-resolved simulations reproduce the predicted motion, conservation of sector weights, and local probability additivity, including repeated spatial overlaps. We also derive the local Grover action for an arbitrary partition into blocks of possibly unequal sizes, explicitly describing how their means are redistributed while each zero-sum deviation remains within its block and changes sign. The framework provides direct control of propagation and trapping within one fixed graph and walk operator through the preparation of the initial state.

title: Hardware-aware sampling and QPU-informed Monte Carlo with quantum annealers
abstract: We study how the physical representation of a logical model affects sampling by quantum annealers and its use in corrected Monte Carlo. The square-lattice Ising model provides controlled classical references. Fixed embeddings with one physical qubit per logical spin reach $36\times36$ spins. Comparisons with uniform two-qubit chains and mixed chain lengths show that matching mean energy leaves differences in magnetization and correlations. Extended-range conditional predictors improve the description of mixed embeddings, distinguishing their residual correlations from those of the tested uniform embeddings. Independent calibration checks and fixed-scale annealing scans show that temperature shifts alone do not determine distributional agreement. Normalized autoregressive models learned from QPU samples provide proposals with exact Metropolis--Hastings and multiple-try corrections on larger periodic lattices. These preserve the target distribution, although block updates alone relax critical magnetization slowly. Complementary direct-QPU updates reveal how block size and fitted-temperature correction affect acceptance and spin motion. Together, the results support prioritizing one-qubit representations and short uniform chains, while separating hardware sampling fidelity from the convergence of corrected Monte Carlo.

title: Underlying orbital U(1) symmetry in quantum limit cycles
abstract: Quantum limit cycles exhibit harmonic Liouvillian spectra, yet their underlying orbital $U(1)$ structure is not generally explicit in the absence of physical rotational symmetry. Here, we construct a unitary representation of orbital phase translations through a similarity transformation that maps the harmonic nondecaying Liouvillian sector onto a Hermitian angular-momentum Hamiltonian. The resulting phase states possess homogeneous Fubini--Study geometry independently of the physical orbit's shape. For ideal quantum limit cycles, the corresponding density matrix also exhibit homogeneous Bures geometry. At finite size, we show how phase diffusion damps slow Liouvillian harmonics while preserving the effective orbital $U(1)$ symmetry. The resulting loss of phase-state distinguishability and contraction of the effective geometry are quantitatively predicted by the microscopic slow Liouvillian spectrum. Our results establish a connection between orbital phase symmetry, quantum geometry, and finite-size phase diffusion in open quantum systems.

title: Hybrid Uncertainty in the Real Forms of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$
abstract: An optimized commutator bound can lie strictly below the quantum infimum even when its minimizing mean is realized by a quantum state. We study hybrid uncertainty, defined as the sum of pairwise products of standard deviations. For any spanning list of nonzero real linear combinations of the generators in a positive discrete series representation of $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$, the commutator bound has a unique minimizing mean, realized by a Perelomov coherent state. We prove that the optimized bound equals the infimum over states with finite second moments if and only if the symmetrized covariance matrix of the prescribed observables is diagonal in this state. When this condition fails, the quantum infimum is strictly greater than the bound; for a nonorthogonal list, we obtain an explicit positive lower bound on this gap. For irreducible spin-$j$ representations of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, we derive the exact minimum of the spectral hybrid uncertainty over states for any spanning list of spin observables. For a fixed state, we compare separate measurements made before a random target is disclosed with direct measurement of the target known in advance. For these protocols, the excess mean squared error coefficient equals twice the listed hybrid uncertainty, and its minimum over orthogonal combinations of the observables equals twice the spectral hybrid uncertainty.

title: Indefinite causal order with definite Bohmian trajectories for the quantum switch
abstract: We analyze the notion of indefinite causal order (ICO) from the standpoint of the deterministic de Broglie--Bohm theory, based on the notion of trajectories in configuration space. More precisely, we study the physics of the quantum switch (QS) interferometer within a Bohmian framework and show how the notion of causality is preserved in this approach. Furthermore, we investigate device-independent certification and causal inequalities applied to an entangled quantum system, and show that in this regime too, the notions of trajectories and of a strict causal order are perfectly preserved.

title: Data re-uploading in Quantum Reservoir Computing
abstract: Data re-uploading enhances the learnable function space of parameterized quantum circuits and has become standard practice in circuit-based \ac{qml}. Its role in quantum reservoir computing, however, remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce data re-uploading into physical quantum reservoir computing and show that repeated input encoding significantly enhances the learnability of higher-order nonlinear polynomials and improves performance on chaotic time-series prediction tasks. We consider protocols with either fixed or increasing computational cost and compare them with a complementary dissipative protocol to distinguish the effects of repeated input encoding from those of additional state overwriting. Using the information processing capacity framework, we identify a memory--nonlinearity trade-off: increasing the number of encodings shifts capacity toward higher-order nonlinearities. In contrast, the dissipative protocol does not extend the range of learnable nonlinear orders and yields only limited improvements in task performance. These results establish data re-uploading as an effective means of tuning and enhancing nonlinear processing in physical quantum reservoir computing.

title: Dissipation-induced integrability in a spin-1 chain and a Bose-Hubbard mixture
abstract: We construct a nonintegrable spin-1 chain that acquires a Yang--Baxter integrable no-jump Hamiltonian through a single dissipative channel per bond. Energy is the only nontrivial finite-range charge of the isolated periodic bulk. Interference cancels the reverse spin conversions, leaving directed moves that obey nil-Coxeter relations and generate commuting charges of increasing range on the open chain. We obtain the full Liouvillian spectrum at any chain length and identify an exponentially large set of blocked spin configurations whose superpositions are all stationary. Resolving the bond outputs leaves the no-jump Hamiltonian unchanged; each bond on which two configurations differ then contributes equally to their dephasing. In a two-component Bose--Hubbard chain, opposite loss phases produce counterpropagating species whose motion and collisions enter a common transfer matrix when interspecies attraction matches intraspecies repulsion. At this coupling, redistributing a pair costs no interaction energy in the atomic limit. Such bond interference offers a route to integrability in other open quantum many-body systems.

title: Efficient representations by PEPS: critical free-fermion and chiral topological states
abstract: We construct projected entangled-pair state (PEPS) approximations to various many-body states in 2D lattices with global error at most $ε$ and bond dimension polynomial in the system size and $1/ε$. They include critical free-fermion models in two dimensions, as well as chiral topological states. For the two-dimensional nearest-neighbor tight-binding model at half filling, our construction combines Gaussian wavelet transformations with matrix product state approximations of the one-dimensional chains, as well as selected fermionic swap operations. For arbitrary uniformly gapped, finite-range quadratic Hamiltonians, we give a different construction based on repeated one-particle filtering, which yields Gaussian PEPS in any spatial dimension. Those include, for instance, $p+ip$ models or a Chern-insulator in a square lattice, for which we give an explicit construction. Finally, we prove that Gutzwiller projections of a fixed number of identical Gaussian PEPS approximations to free-fermion states at arbitrary filling do not amplify considerably the approximation error. This provides a polynomial-bond PEPS approximations to the resulting states, including familiar lattice chiral-spin-liquid states.

title: Benchmarking superconducting quantum processors with percolating entanglement quality
abstract: The capability to create large entanglement resources is a key performance attribute of quantum processors, and the size of the resource is often used as a benchmark of processor scale. Recent graph-state experiments have reported entanglement clusters spanning entire chips with hundreds of qubits. However, cluster size alone does not capture the entanglement quality of individual couplings or differences in coupling topology. Here, we introduce percolating entanglement quality (PEQ), a topology-normalized benchmark based on conditional two-qubit negativity and a topology-specific bond-percolation threshold. As an experimental demonstration, we prepare a native graph state on a 64-qubit square-lattice superconducting processor with defects, identify a 52-qubit entanglement cluster, and evaluate the PEQ of the processor. Applying PEQ to previously reported chip-wide graph-state measurements on heavy-hex-lattice processors, we show that PEQ differs substantially among processors whose entanglement clusters span the entire chip. PEQ provides a single chip-wide score without selecting a best-performing qubit subset or path. This score allows processors with different coupling topologies to be compared on a common scale and can inform the design of coupling topologies for scalable chips.

title: Local Quantum Metrology: Precision Limits for Observers in QFT
abstract: How precisely can an observer estimate a parameter related to a quantum field? This question is answered for quantum-mechanical systems using the SLD--Bures--Fisher metric and the quantum Cramér--Rao bound. However, local algebras in relativistic quantum field theory are of type III: they carry no trace and normal states have no density matrices, so the SLD quantum Fisher information and the quantum Cramér--Rao bound cannot be defined in the usual way. We define the SLD (Bures) quantum Fisher information on arbitrary von Neumann algebras through Uhlmann's transition probability and prove a quantum Cramér--Rao bound for collective measurements. We also show that the bound is sharp, and equals the largest classical Fisher information obtainable by measurements in the region.

title: Digital Coherent Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution with Gaussian-Modulated Coherent States
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) enables information-theoretically secure key sharing between two distant parties. Recently, one promising QKD protocol which can distribute a secret key over long distances called twin-field QKD (TF-QKD) has been developed. However, it requires active compensation for experimental imperfections such as phase, polarization, and frequency fluctuations with expensive devices and this makes its experimental implementation challenging. Here, we propose a long-distance continuous-variable QKD (CV-QKD) protocol which is inspired by TF-QKD. Our protocol can remove these requirements by using Gaussian-modulated coherent states and digital signal processing which is widely used in recent digital coherent optical communication and experimental implementations of CV-QKD. For security analysis, we use a numerical optimization approach with a photon-number cutoff assumption. We propose a new set of constraints for numerical optimization which can efficiently constrain a highly non-Gaussian quantum state shared by two legitimate parties in our protocol. We show that the key rate of our protocol exceeds the key rate of a direct-transmission CV-QKD protocol at long distances and it can overcome the repeaterless bound.

title: A Concise Introduction to Quantum Electromagnetics
abstract: This book introduces quantum electromagnetics to readers trained in classical electromagnetics, without assuming a systematic background in quantum mechanics. The central question is when classical descriptions suffice, and when the quantum states of matter or the field must be retained explicitly. Starting from familiar electromagnetic modes and material response, the discussion develops atomic dynamics, field quantization, and the interaction of quantized fields with quantum matter. Particular attention is given to how mode profiles, Green functions, and scattering matrices obtained from classical electromagnetic calculations enter quantum models. Atomic coherence, photon statistics, spontaneous emission, and cavity coupling are developed through derivations that identify the physical assumptions and limits of each description. Examples drawn from atomic clocks, Rydberg-atom receivers, and single-photon devices connect these concepts to excitation, propagation, and measurement in practical systems. Loss and noise are included in relating internal dynamics to measured signals and correlations. The final discussion examines how sensitivity and claims of quantum advantage depend on bandwidth, measurement resources, and the classical reference used for comparison. The aim is to help readers choose an appropriate model, carry out the calculation, and understand what its predictions mean for an electromagnetic measurement.

title: The cone of states over time: exact tests and convergent two-sided hierarchies
abstract: A state over time (stote) pairs a state $ρ$ with a channel $\mathcal{E}$ as the Hermitian, generally non-positive operator $(ρ\otimes\mathbf{1})\star J_\mathcal{E}$. We study the convex cone $\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}$ generated by these operators. Our main result is a convergent outer semidefinite hierarchy with an explicit trace-norm Hausdorff bound on its trace-one slices. Specializing constrained symmetric-extension theory to the input--channel representation, we show that Bose-extension rounding preserves the channel marginal constraint and gives error at most $2d_A^2(d_A-1)/(k+d_A-1)$ at level $k$. A complementary inner hierarchy retains all channels at each chosen pure-input direction. For $d_A\ge2$, its error is at most $2(d_A-1)\sin^2δ$, where $δ$ is the Fubini--Study covering radius; nested sets of $N$ directions give error at most $2π^2(d_A-1)N^{-1/(d_A-1)}$, independently of $d_B$. These bounds provide explicit size--accuracy guarantees and certified support-value bounds, without guaranteeing finite termination for exact boundary membership. For binary classical outputs, we obtain an exact SDP membership test, including indefinite output blocks and mixtures that are not single stotes. At faithful marginal the test reduces to a scalar inequality; every trace-one member of this sector with input marginal $ρ$ has a constructive realization using at most $\operatorname{rank}ρ$ pure-input stotes with binary measurement channels. Finally, we compute the exact isotropic boundary and prove $\mathrm{PPT}\subsetneq\widehat{\mathcal{Q}}\cap\mathrm{PSD}\subsetneq\mathrm{PSD}$ for equal local dimensions at least two.

title: Max-Cut QAOA on Non-Hardware-Native Graphs via MinLA Surrogates and Configuration Recovery
abstract: For non-hardware-native \textsc{MAX-CUT} instances, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can incur additional two-qubit depth overhead due to SWAP-based routing of interactions between non-adjacent qubits. We propose a hybrid quantum--classical workflow that reduces this depth by selectively removing interactions and subsequently recovers solution quality through classical optimization of the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We employ a Minimum Linear Arrangement (MinLA)-based vertex ordering to preferentially retain short-range interactions, thereby constructing a two-qubit depth-reduced surrogate QAOA ansatz. To compensate for the information lost through interaction removal, we develop classical \textit{recovery} strategies that refine QPU-sampled bitstrings directly on the original \textsc{MAX-CUT} objective. We develop two recovery strategies: signed-residue-based local search and bipartite-block optimization, where each conditional block problem is solved exactly using an $s$--$t$ minimum cut. Recovery is performed independently on each sampled configuration, ensuring monotonic improvement in cut value without additional QPU executions. We evaluate the workflow on \texttt{ibm\_kingston} for 120 distinct non-hardware-native instances comprising $6$-regular and Erdős--Rényi graphs with 40, 60 and 100 vertices. We verify that the surrogates substantially reduce transpiled two-qubit depth while staying within the prescribed two-qubit depth, and with recovery yield \textit{near-optimal} cuts on the original graphs. These results demonstrate the potential of hardware-aware interaction selection and classical recovery to extend QAOA to graph instances whose full cost Hamiltonians exceed practical circuit-depth budgets.

title: Quantum kinetic uncertainty relations: Role of coherence in current fluctuation bounds
abstract: We present a comparative analysis of three quantum versions of the kinetic uncertainty relation (KUR), which incorporate coherence-dependent corrections to the classical bound. Using a three-level maser heat engine as a paradigmatic quantum thermal machine, we identify the operating regimes in which each formulation provides the tightest constraint on current fluctuations. We further identify tighter, model-specific bounds for two of these formulations, provide numerical support for both, and establish one of them analytically. Introducing ground-state degeneracy, we then demonstrate that noise-induced coherence provides a tunable resource for relocating, enhancing, or suppressing violations of the standard KUR without requiring an additional coherent drive. In particular, it enables violations in regimes where the three-level engine satisfies the classical bound. Our results clarify how distinct quantum KURs account for coherence and constrain the precision of quantum thermal machines.

title: Hidden Quantum Markov Processes: Mealy Formulation and Observable Reduction
abstract: We formulate hidden quantum Markov processes in a Mealy architecture using a single completely positive unital transition expectation coupling the present hidden system, the emitted output, and the next hidden system. Together with a boundary state, it generates a quasi-local, finitely correlated hidden--output state; for the commutative generator associated with a classical Mealy kernel, this state is the full joint law of the classical Mealy model.   Moore realizations correspond to transition expectations that factor on the prescribed hidden algebra. We establish a rank obstruction to such factorization and prove its sufficiency for isometric generators: factorization holds exactly when the induced hidden-memory channel has Kraus rank at most the hidden Hilbert-space dimension. The Kraus rank also gives the minimal intermediate Hilbert-space dimension. When the hidden and output dimensions are at least two, the factorizable isometric generators form a closed subset of measure zero.   For any fixed projective readout, a Mealy generator induces an operational hidden quantum Markov model in the sense of Monràs, Beige and Wiesner; conversely, every finite-dimensional operational model admits a Mealy lift on the same memory space with a rank-one readout. For their cluster-state instrument, two isometric, Moore-factorizable lifts with the same instrument and initial memory state yield identical measured output statistics but different quantum output states: one has marginals entangled across $1|2\cdots n$ for $n\geq3$, with three-output negativity $\tfrac12$, whereas the other has fully separable marginals. Thus operational equivalence does not determine output entanglement.

title: Linear-optical generation of approximate higher-component cat states
abstract: We propose a method for generating higher-component cat states by interfering two $N$-component cat states on a half beam splitter and measuring one output with a photon-number-resolving detector. The Fock components of the conditional output are restricted to a single residue class modulo $2N$. For $N=3$, an ideal six-component cat state can be generated exactly, while for arbitrary $N$, the conditional output approaches an ideal $2N$-component cat state for sufficiently large input amplitudes.

title: Spin-adapted sample-based quantum diagonalization with randomized time evolution
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on the classical post-processing of measurement samples have emerged as effective and robust methods to approximate low-energy wavefunctions of many-body quantum systems on present-day and early-fault-tolerant quantum devices. This paper introduces a generic framework for enforcing spin symmetry within these approaches. We tailor this framework to SqDRIFT, a sample-based quantum diagonalization variant that uses the qDRIFT randomized compilation protocol to generate the quantum samples. We discuss how three key components of SqDRIFT (the initial-state preparation, the construction of the time-evolution circuits, and the classical post-processing) can be adapted to incorporate spin symmetry. We show that spin-pure circuits alone are not sufficient, since the sampled determinants generally span a subspace that is not closed under $\hat{S}^2$, and we restore this closure by completing the sampled electronic configurations. In classical simulations of 4-aminobenzonitrile and of an $[\text{Fe}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ model complex, and in experiments on an IBM quantum processor for the oxo-Mn(Salen) complex, this spin-adapted post-processing yields roots that are exact spin eigenfunctions at every subspace size. On hardware, it does so with diagonalized subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of the conventional constructions for the same circuit depth.

title: Hybrid Krotov gradient descent Optimization for Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: We introduce and study a Krotov-inspired discrete adjoint optimization scheme for quantum machine learning and focus on a hybrid online-to-batch schedule. The method transfers the forward/costate/local-update logic of continuous-time optimal control to parameterized quantum circuits by replacing time locality with gate-index locality. For a broad class of fixed-generator variational gates and terminal-state losses, we show that the batch Krotov direction coincides with the exact gradient of the empirical loss. Under standard smoothness assumptions, this yields monotonic descent and convergence of the batch method, and convergence of the tail of the hybrid method after a finite switch to the batch phase. Empirically, we benchmark hybrid Krotov against the tuned PennyLane optimizer suite and L-BFGS-B on a four-bit parity classifier and on the Pérez-Salinas data re-uploading classifier for the crown problem. Across matched hyperparameter sweeps with three seeds per configuration, hybrid Krotov dominates every tuned first-order baseline and matches the strongest structured PennyLane methods on parity, while approaching the accuracy of L-BFGS-B on Pérez-Salinas at first-order per-iteration cost.

title: Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications
abstract: Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones. Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of $(j-1)$ quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of $j$ registers (of $n_{qb}$ qubits each) using a mere $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ $\mathtt{CNOT}$ and single-qubit gates, and $3j+\lceil\log_2j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''. The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of \cite{Galvez-Viruet:2024hry} by almost two powers of $j$ and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.

title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
abstract: Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

title: Quantum Preparation without Disturbance: Information Costs and Hypothesis Testing
abstract: We determine the minimum information cost of preparing either of two quantum states with one common device while preserving its memory. Measured by the Umegaki relative entropy between the two possible memory states, this minimum is the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy of the target states. If the memory may instead be consumed, the minimum is their Umegaki relative entropy. More generally, for any divergence satisfying data processing, memory preservation selects the maximal extension of its classical restriction. We also study the cost of requiring only finitely many outputs, with the costs increasing from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy as the number of outputs grows. Finally, we consider hypothesis testing of an unknown device over independent runs. The optimal Stein exponent per run converges to the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy whenever the number of outputs per run diverges. This gives an operational characterization of the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy in quantum statistics.

title: Entropic quantum error correction for independent and correlated amplitude damping errors
abstract: The idea of using quantum entropy for quantum error correction (QEC) has existed for a long time. However, its computational complexity has limited its practical use: even a $[[4,1]]$ code for standard independent amplitude damping errors involves a $256\times 256$ Hermitian matrix, so the approach scales poorly as the codeword length increases. For correlated errors, the situation is even worse. In this paper, we show that, by using the insights developed in our previous paper and exploiting certain structures of quantum conditional mutual information, we can solve these problems exactly by hand, using only $2\times 2$ unitary matrices. By examining the entropy, we identify the leakage channels and the amount of leakage exactly, then define the recovery map accordingly. The rules defining our recovery map are simple, intuitive, and computationally inexpensive: for independent errors, it is based on 16 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions; for correlated errors, it is based on 6 explicitly given orthonormal vectors and 6 instructions. Our method sacrifices little in terms of performance: for the widely used entanglement fidelity, our simple QEC recovery map achieves a sharp result; for the worst-case fidelity, the best result is about $9\%$ better than ours; for correlated errors, there are no comparable results for short codewords. Among the known techniques, our recovery map is the first non-global one. The calculations use elementary linear algebra and calculus, and is presented in great detail.

title: Spin Interferometry Generated by Cavity Memory
abstract: We report the control and observation of coherent spin interferometry generated by cavity memory using an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers coupled to a microwave cavity. The abrupt switch-on and switch-off of a detuned drive produce transient fields at the cavity frequency that supply the two spin rotations for Ramsey interferometry, observed using both microwave and fluorescence readout. Spectrally scanning the spin profile across the cavity and drive frequencies distinguishes cavity-generated Ramsey interference from conventional Rabi dynamics. Temporal weighting of the reflected microwave signal enables spectrally selective population readout at a single probe frequency. By programming the phase and amplitude of the drive envelope, we extend the same mechanism to more quantum control sequences, including spin-echo and Rabi control.

title: Maximally Entangled Mutually Unbiased Bases in Bipartite Systems of Unequal Prime Dimensions
abstract: Mutually unbiased bases with prescribed entanglement properties are of fundamental interest in quantum information theory. In the interesting case of a bipartite Hilbert space of unequal prime dimensions, $\mathcal{H}_p\otimes\mathcal{H}_q$, with $p<q$ prime, the standard solution provides $p+1$ product bases. For any such dimension $d=pq$ we construct $p+1$ bases, such that $p$ of them are represented by complex Hadamard matrices, each equivalent to a Fourier matrix $F_d$, with all vectors maximally entangled. Our explicit construction is based on eigenvectors of suitable Weyl--Heisenberg operators, the Chinese Remainder Theorem and quadratic Gaussian sums. The obtained result establishes a lower bound for the number of maximally entangled mutually unbiased bases, $M(p,q)\geq p$.

title: An Incomplete-Preference Quantum Anscombe--Aumann Representation
abstract: This work develops a generalised Anscombe--Aumann framework in which acts map a finite set of states of the world into the effect interval of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, while preferences need not be complete. The construction keeps three logically distinct questions separate. First, an incomplete-preference multi-utility theorem supplies affine utility functionals. Second, finite-dimensional operator geometry determines the form of each affine functional. Third, admissibility identifies which normalised probability--state pairs are compatible with the full preference. We introduce behavioural state-independence as the natural Anscombe--Aumann interpretation of the idea that the identity of the states of the world should not affect how quantum consequences are compared. Because an incomplete preference makes this aggregate behavioural condition weaker than a utility-by-utility condition, the factorisation theorem requires a stronger, explicitly operational representation-level condition. Under that condition and Loewner monotonicity, every affine utility functional is positively affinely equivalent to a normalised utility of the form $U_{p,ρ}(f)=\sum_{s}p(s)Tr(ρf(s))$. Consequently, a suitable incomplete preference relation is represented by a family of admissible pairs in $Δ(S) \times \mathcal{D} ( \mathcal{H} ) $. We then identify a canonical maximal compatible family and show that the scalar-effect subspace carries an ordinary classical multi-utility representation, with scalar events appearing as the vertices of the scalar-act cube.

title: Fer expansion converges almost twice as far as Magnus for qubits
abstract: The Fer expansion writes the propagator of a time-dependent Hamiltonian as a product of unitary exponentials whose error decreases doubly exponentially with the number of factors, while the Magnus expansion improves by one order at a time. Its convergence, however, was guaranteed only below a radius of about $2.6058$, smaller than the Magnus radius $π$. We establish a guaranteed convergence threshold of about $6.2106$, or $1.98\,π$, for a qubit. This is almost twice the optimal universal Magnus threshold $π$; the bound on a single Fer step is sharp, while the exact convergence radius remains open.

title: Observing Enhanced Entanglement in an Ising Quantum Register Beyond Weak Measurement
abstract: Measurements often yield a disentangled quantum state which is the most probable measurement outcome while the measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement could be exponentially less probable or absent. Higher probability in measurement outcomes with enhanced entanglement is virtue in experimental observation of enhance entanglement in post-selected or Born-rule measurements with less resources in noisy quantum devices. We develop a periodic measurement sampling(PMS) protocol in the framework of uniform matrix product states. Using PMS, we identify a peak enhancement of entanglement in a uniform post-measurement state whose probabilistic outcome can be maximized by optimizing a measurement super-cell. A measurement super-cell is the smallest repeating building block of qubits defined by the measurement density, external field strength and exchange interactions between quantum register and ancilla qubits. The above prediction based on a classical description of the many-body quantum state is demonstrated in a quantum computing experiment in a loop of quantum register qubits with Ising interactions in the presence of transverse magnetic field. Further, we show the scalability of predictions of the periodic measurement sampling protocol in the thermodynamic limit to finite size systems. Especially, we present a rescaling ansatz which would enable predicting the possibility of observing enhanced entanglement in finite size systems.

title: Chip-Based Discrete-Modulated Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution with Uncertainty-Principle-Based Composable Security
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution offers a promising platform for scalable quantum networks through its compatibility with standard telecommunications technology and photonic integration. High-order discrete modulation facilitates practical implementation while approaching the key-rate performance of ideal Gaussian modulation, but its finite-size composable security analysis entails substantial computational overhead. Here, we develop an uncertainty-principle-based security framework that enables finite-size composable key-rate evaluation against collective attacks for constellations up to 256-QAM. By introducing a heterodyne-measured ancillary mode into the entanglement-based source description, we incorporate additional source correlations into the security analysis that allow the Heisenberg uncertainty principle alone to provide a tight bound for the unknown correlations in a covariance matrix characterizing the whole system. Matrix symmetrization further reduces the key-rate optimization to a one-dimensional search, while subsequent mode reduction yields an analytical lower bound requiring no numerical search. Experimental demonstrations using 256-QAM on discrete-component and silicon-photonic-receiver platforms achieve finite-size composable secret key rates of 17.436 and 0.519 Mbps, respectively, over a 50 km fiber link. This approach facilitates the practical deployment of high-speed, real-time and compact quantum key distribution systems. Beyond quantum key distribution, the principle of tightening uncertainty-constrained bounds via source-mode expansion offers a paradigm for exploring the information-theoretic properties of complex non-Gaussian systems.

title: Formulating Uncomputation Beyond Classical Ancilla Use
abstract: Ancilla qubits are routinely used to simplify quantum circuit construction and reduce implementation costs, but their use introduces the burden of designing proper uncomputation afterward. To alleviate this, prior work has developed automated uncomputation synthesis based on a computational-basis formulation of ancilla use. However, this formulation is tailored to classically structured ancilla computations. For more general circuits, it may be undefined, yield unintended functionality, or fail to synthesize uncomputation. It therefore falls short of providing a precise and general formulation of uncomputation beyond classical ancilla use.   To address these limitations, we propose a new formulation of ancilla use that specifies the operation of each gate through two complementary aspects: (1) the functionality it implements and (2) the transformation it induces on ancilla roles. Based on this specification, we define uncomputation as restoring the initial ancilla role while implementing the identity functionality. This perspective enables a simple Use-first strategy for automatically synthesizing uncomputation in cases both within and beyond the scope of prior approaches. We further develop a complete inference system for reasoning about specifications, together with a derivation-directed procedure for automatically synthesizing efficient uncomputation, enabling systematic uncomputation synthesis even in challenging cases beyond the scope of our automatic strategy.

title: Quantum thermometry with k-local Hamiltonians
abstract: In equilibrium quantum thermometry, the precision of temperature estimation increases with the heat capacity of the probe thermometer. For an n-body thermometer, the maximum heat capacity is attained by a Hamiltonian that requires n-local interactions, making its physical implementation challenging. In the thermodynamic limit, the optimal heat capacity scales quadratically with n. Although more experimentally accessible 2-local Hamiltonians can achieve this optimal scaling, their performance remains significantly below the theoretical maximum for realistic system sizes. Here, we restrict to this scenario and show a substantial enhancement in the thermometric performance with only a minimal increase in locality in some Hamiltonian models. We further introduce k-local generalizations of these models and show that their thermometric performance systematically approaches the theoretical optimum as the locality is increased. By analyzing their spectra, we relate this enhancement to the progressive emergence of the spectral structure underlying optimal equilibrium thermometry. Lastly, we discuss the heat capacity as a witness of Hamiltonian locality.

title: Efficient Parameter Estimation through Quantum Extreme Learning
abstract: Quantum sensing protocols rely on the efficient processing of measurement outcomes to infer unknown physical parameters. Conventional optimal estimators, such as Bayesian inference and maximum likelihood estimation, require to construct a likelihood function whose efficient classical construction requires full knowledge of the dynamics, which may practically be infeasible. Model-free experimental construction of the likelihood is also very resource intensive. Here, we propose a quantum extreme learning-based framework for quantum parameter estimation which avoids the explicit construction of the likelihood function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using the transverse-field Ising model for estimating the external transverse field. Our results show that high estimation accuracy can be achieved using measurements at only a small number of training points. We further develop an interrogation-time optimization strategy that minimizes the estimation inaccuracy while keeping sampling fluctuations below a prescribed threshold. We further extend the framework to a two-time measurement protocol, in which measurement outcomes obtained at two distinct times are combined to enrich the feature space, thereby significantly enhancing the estimation accuracy. Our analysis shows that the estimation precision improves monotonically with the number of training points, while increasing the system size generally enhances the sensing performance, albeit non-monotonically. Finally, the protocol is shown to be robust against dephasing, making it suitable for near-term quantum devices.

title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states $ρ$ and observables $\mathcal{M}$ by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form $2$-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if $ρ^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance $τ$ with the number of runs polynomial in $1/τ$, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.

title: Quantum computational spectroscopy of complex resonances and optical residues
abstract: Optical spectra of dissipative molecular systems depend on both complex resonance energies and the way each resonance couples to an optical probe. In a non-Hermitian description, these con- tributions are determined by complex residues involving left and right eigenvectors. We introduce a quantum protocol that reconstructs the resonance poles and their biorthogonal optical residues within a common spectral-filtering and measurement framework. A Hermitian dilation embeds the left and right eigenvectors into a zero-energy subspace. Gaussian-filtered correlators evaluated with unitary circuits, together with ratios of complex off-diagonal measurements, yield the residues with- out separate variational optimisation of the eigenstates. We demonstrate spectral reconstruction for dissipative plasmon-molecule models on IBM quantum hardware, resolving how probe-dependent modal contributions produce interference-induced doublets or accompany a separation of resonance energies. We also analyse the sensitivity of residue reconstruction near exceptional points. By mak- ing complex optical residues an explicit computational output, the protocol connects non-Hermitian eigenstructure to measurable optical response.

title: Number fluctuations and particle loss in Dicke superradiance
abstract: Dicke superradiance, the collective spontaneous emission of identical quantum emitters into a common reservoir, produces a burst with a characteristic delay $t_{\mathrm{SR}}$ and a peak intensity that scales quadratically with the emitter number $N$. This strong dependence makes the burst sensitive to how many emitters actually participate. In experiments, however, this number is rarely fixed: it fluctuates between preparations and decreases during emission through atom loss. Here we extend the analytical treatment of superradiance to variable emitter numbers using the Schwinger-boson mapping of the collective spin onto two bosonic modes. In this formulation, collective decay annihilates an atom in the excited-state mode and creates one in the ground-state mode. We find that number fluctuations enhance emission and that the ensemble-averaged emission trace encodes the initial number distribution. We show how to reconstruct second-order correlations from photon counting with finite detection efficiency and temporal resolution, even when the full distribution cannot be resolved. For atom loss at rate $r$, we derive exact results for the population dynamics and show that the peak intensity scaling is governed by the single scaling variable $g_{\mathrm{r}}=r t_{\mathrm{SR}}$. The peak remains quadratic in $N$ for $g_{\mathrm{r}}<1$, follows logarithmically corrected subquadratic power laws for $g_{\mathrm{r}}>1$, and crosses over to linear scaling under strong loss with $g_{\mathrm{r}}\gg1$.

title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
abstract: We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.

title: Nesting in additive manufacturing using quantum annealing
abstract: Nesting in powder bed fusion (PBF), an additive manufacturing (AM) process, determines the positions and orientations of parts within the build space and influences build height and build time. As the number of parts and feasible placements increases, the nesting problem becomes computationally demanding. Exact approaches are limited to small problem sizes as computational effort increases rapidly with the problem size, while heuristic and metaheuristic approaches involve a trade-off between solution quality and computation time. Quantum annealing (QA) offers an alternative for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its application to nesting in AM remains largely unexplored.
